Is D-Wave's quantum computer an actual quantum computer?

The D-Wave is definitely a real quantum computer, but it isn't a general quantum computer.

To start, let's draw a distinction between a quantum computer and a traditional computer that isn't also a quick intro to quantum mechanics and spin.

Computing is, at its core, about symbolic operations, that represent something useful about real events. If people are walking by you in a stadium, that's a real event--and if you count them on an abacus in your hand as they walk by, then that's computing. You're correlating the physical event (person walks by) with a symbolic action that represents it (move this bead across this wire), and then at the end, you can look at your model and say something about the world. "Forty-seven people passed me today."

So, an abacus is an example of a classical computer, because moving a bead from one end of a string to the other is 'classical physics'. All modern 'classical' computers are kinda like tiny abaci that use electrons as the beads. This is a classical effect because the electrons are just being sucked from one end of a silicon-and-copper maze to the other, and being normal particles all the way. The color of each pixel on your monitor is driven by the presence or absence of electrons in a bunch of little wells, so you can 'math' on it and get things like voat or your favorite pr0nz to appear on the screen.

The debate about the D-Wave was about whether it models quantum physics, or whether it measures quantum physics. It was believed by some that, in essence, the D-Wave was a very sophisticated "quantum mechanics emulator" built entirely out of classical bits. You could just think of it as a crazy-overclocked Intel processor that was playing 'Quantum Mechanics: The Game': it would produce the same results as a quantum system, but ultimately, it would just be doing classical physics in order to carry out math about quantum systems. Each 'operation' of the processor would consist of, 'move this electrical charge from here to there'.

It's fairly clear today that the D-Wave actually solves optimization problems with real quantum systems. So, instead of arranging a bunch of electrons in the right wells (transistors) like you would in a classical system, you arrange a bunch of qubits and entangle them with one another in such a way that their entanglement is representative of the problem you're computing. This is the 'input' stage. So, then, the qubits all settle into place, the system 'balances' and whatnot, and then, you measure some properties of those qubits. Those properties will have been determined by the shape of the entanglement patterns you set up in the input stage.

So, classical computers use classical physics to do all the things they do. The D-Wave is a real quantum computer, even though it is not a general quantum computer, because it uses quantum physics to do its calculations.

Basically, the whole “many calculations” explanation is bullshit. Here’s a better explanation of specifically that part.

In order to guess the private key of an encrypted key pair, on a classical system, you have to verify each possible key until one works. This is the “brute force” attack. So, the classical computer tries key after key after key.

The quantum computer, on the other hand, creates a 2D surface (sometimes called the ‘energy landscape’ for this kind of problem) which represents the possible values of the key. Then, it measures what point on the surface has the highest energy, and says, “Ah, that corresponds to 0xdeadbeef420, which is your correct private key”.

The quantumness of the qubits mostly comes down to the fact that you can entangle neighbor qubits with one another in interesting ways, which is how you affect what the “energy landscape” is shaped like before you measure it to find your solution.
